verses.text: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:
a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted;
a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;
a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;
a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away;
a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;
a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.
What profit has he who works in that in which he labors?
I have seen the burden which God has given to the sons of men to be afflicted with.
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.
I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice, and to do good as long as they live.
Also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy good in all his labor, is the gift of God.
I know that whatever God does, it shall be forever. Nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it; and God has done it, that men should fear before him.
That which is has been long ago, and that which is to be has been long ago: and God seeks again that which is passed away.
Moreover I saw under the sun, in the place of justice, that wickedness was there; and in the place of righteousness, that wickedness was there.
I said in my heart, “God will judge the righteous and the wicked; for there is a time there for every purpose and for every work.”
I said in my heart, “As for the sons of men, God tests them, so that they may see that they themselves are like animals.

For that which happens to the sons of men happens to animals. Even one thing happens to them. As the one dies, so the other dies. Yes, they have all one breath; and man has no advantage over the animals: for all is vanity.
All go to one place. All are from the dust, and all turn to dust again.
Who knows the spirit of man, whether it goes upward, and the spirit of the animal, whether it goes downward to the earth?”
Therefore I saw that there is nothing better, than that a man should rejoice in his works; for that is his portion: for who can bring him to see what will be after him?

footnotes.content: How simple and true—everything has its moment, under the eye of God who holds time itself. I've watched this play out across a long life: the wrong thing at the wrong hour brings only grief, while the same thing in its proper season blooms like spring rain on thirsty ground. Even our sorrows and joys make sense when we stop fighting the rhythm He set.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Birth and death, planting and harvest—the poles of our small story. I've stood with families at both ends, and always there's a rightness to it when we don't rage but receive it. The seed must go into the ground; the plant must be pulled up. Life moves in this rhythm, and our peace comes from trusting the Gardener.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To kill and heal, to break and rebuild—not all of this belongs to us, but all of it speaks to God's work. I've known surgeons and carpenters, soldiers and those tending wounds; each finds holiness when they're faithful to their hour. The breaking down makes no sense without the building up that follows—and Jesus, our greatest Builder, came broken first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tears and laughter, sorrow and dance—both real, both necessary. I've learned not to despise the weeping season; it teaches us depths. And the dancing—oh, how it lifts us. The Christian life isn't a smile painted on, but a heart that knows how to grieve truly and then, by grace, to whirl in the light again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There's wisdom in knowing when to let go of what we've gathered, and when to hold close. The stones we cast away—grudges, the weight we carry—make room for the embrace. In Jesus we learn this most clearly: let go of your own rightness and you'll find arms that hold you whole.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seeking and losing, keeping and casting away—I've found both can be equally hard. The seeking requires hope; the losing requires faith. And sometimes we must cast away even good things to find the better thing. Christ teaches us this: lose your life to find it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Silence and speech—how precious both are, and how often we get them backward. I've sat at the bed of the dying and learned that silence can be louder than words. The Psalms, too, teach us this: sometimes the bravest thing is to keep still, and sometimes the kindest is to speak truth, gentle as it is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Love and hate, war and peace—not as opposites God favors equally, but as seasons a fallen world knows. Our calling isn't to find these balanced but to love God so deeply we hate what hardens us against Him, and to pursue His peace with our whole heart. That's the time we're always in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What gain is there? It's an old question, and I've watched people spend their lives chasing an answer that never quite comes. Then I've watched others find their answer not in the profit of their labor but in the love of God that makes the work itself holy—even the humble work, even the unseen work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God gives us the burden of our labor, yes—and I've carried it, heavy as stone some seasons. But the burden itself is His gift, strangely. Through it we learn to lean, to humble ourselves, to understand that we cannot save ourselves. And that's where He meets us, in our smallness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He's made everything beautiful in its time, yet set eternity in our hearts—this mystery has grown only sweeter to me. We can't grasp the whole of what He's doing, but we can see His fingerprints in every season. And that ache for eternity? That's not a flaw in us; it's Him calling us home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There is nothing better than to rejoice and do good while we live. I've known anxious people who forgot this, waiting for happiness to be worthy of their living. But joy isn't a reward at the end; it's a fruit we bear along the way, most abundant when we're doing good.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To eat, to drink, to find good in our labor—this is God's gift to us, not a temptation to resist. He made us bodies that hunger and thirst; He made work that bears fruit. Gratitude for these simple goods is not vanity; it's worship. This verse has freed many faithful people from needless guilt.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Whatever God does endures forever; nothing can be added or taken away. How it steadies the heart to know this. We fuss and plan and scheme, but His work stands unmoved. He's even made it so that we should fear Him—not in terror, but in awe, in the safety of knowing we're held by One whose purposes cannot fail.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What is has been before; what will be has already been. This sounds strange at first, but it comforts me: I'm not the first to struggle, to doubt, to seek God. Every trial my soul knows, His saints before me have known. And He seeks again what has passed—He remembers, He returns to us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I've seen it too—injustice in the courthouse, wickedness where righteousness should dwell. It breaks something in the soul. But these verses aren't meant to make us despair; they're meant to wake us. We see the rot and are called to be builders of a different kingdom, one not of this world order.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God will judge the righteous and the wicked—this was Qoheleth's comfort, and it should be ours. We don't have to fix everything ourselves or be cynical about justice. He sees. He knows the time for judgment. We can rest in that.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God tests us so we might see we are like the animals—brought down from our high opinion of ourselves. It's humbling, but it's merciful. Pride is what kills us. Knowing our limits, our creatureliness, is the gate to wisdom and to seeing where God truly stands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The same fate befalls all—beast and human alike return to dust. It's stark and true. Yet this is not the end of the story that Jesus came to tell. This is the problem He solves. We share mortality with the animals, but in Him we're given what they cannot have: resurrection.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All go to one place; all come from dust, all turn to dust again. Standing at graves and birth beds, I've felt this truth in my bones. It levels us, strips away pretense. And in that nakedness before God, we find either despair—or faith in the One who can raise dust to life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Who knows if the spirit of a human goes upward or the spirit of an animal goes down? It's a question Qoheleth leaves hanging, and we should too—with reverence and wonder. The mystery itself keeps us humble. Only God knows what lies beyond the veil.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The best good is to rejoice in your works—readers today hear an echo in this ancient counsel. In a time of endless measuring and comparison, we're called back to something simpler: do your work faithfully, find your joy in it, and trust that this is enough. That portion is yours; why look past it?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
